answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: Hebrew text c. 450–180 BCE · King James translation 1611
answer.sourceLine: Ecclesiastes 5:10 in the King James Version (1611), word for word. The full verse ends “…nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.” The book's Hebrew text numbers it 5:9.

source.heading: The verse in the King James Bible
source.excerpt:
5:9 Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field.

5:10 He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.

5:11 When goods increase, they are increased that eat them: and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes?
trail: The Project Gutenberg King James Bible text ↗ gives 5:10 as “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.”
Wikisource's KJV Ecclesiastes ↗ and Blue Letter Bible ↗ have the same wording. Blue Letter Bible also sets it beside dozens of other translations.
In the Hebrew text the verse is numbered 5:9 (Sefaria ↗). It begins אֹהֵב כֶּסֶף לֹא־יִשְׂבַּע כֶּסֶף, which the Revised JPS renders “A lover of money is never satisfied with money.”

Quote Investigator has no page on this line, and Wikiquote's Ecclesiastes page ↗ quotes 5:10 only in the NIV (“Whoever loves money never has money enough…”). The King James Bible itself is the primary source.

author.name: The Preacher (Qoheleth)
author.heading: About The Preacher (Qoheleth)
author.metaLine: Speaker of Ecclesiastes · Hebrew Bible, c. 450–180 BCE
author.bio: “The Preacher” is how the King James Version renders Qoheleth (or Kohelet), the voice of the Book of Ecclesiastes. Wikipedia glosses the name as “someone speaking before an assembly”. Rabbinic tradition credits the book to King Solomon in his old age, but the text never names Solomon. Critical scholars date it to no earlier than about 450 BCE and no later than 180 BCE, when Ben Sira quotes from it.

copyAttribution: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.” — Ecclesiastes 5:10, King James Version (1611)

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is genuine scripture, and there is no famous mix-up over it. But it travels under several names, and it usually travels cut short.

items.why: Rabbinic tradition ↗ holds that Solomon wrote Ecclesiastes in his old age, and many quote sites credit him. The book itself never uses the name Solomon. Critical scholars date it to no earlier than about 450 BCE, centuries after Solomon's reign.
The popular quotation stops at “increase”. The full KJV verse ↗ ends “this is also vanity,” tying it to the book's refrain that such pursuits are vanity.
Lines like “Whoever loves money never has money enough” are the same verse in modern translations such as the NIV (Wikiquote ↗), not a separate saying.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording is the King James Version (1611) of Ecclesiastes 5:10, spoken by “the Preacher” (Qoheleth). See the KJV text on Wikisource ↗.

context.heading: Why the line endures
lead: The verse comes from a run of sayings on wealth in Ecclesiastes 5. The next verse observes that “when goods increase, they are increased that eat them.” Its point is that the love of money cannot be satisfied by getting more of it.

The archaic King James wording (“loveth,” “abundance with increase”) is the form most often quoted in English. Modern translations put the same thought more plainly as a lover of money never having enough.
